Assert Router.Select's smooth-WRR selection converges to skipping the failing deployment entirely while the remaining healthy deployments' relative selection ratio stays exactly proportional to their own configured weights -- Netflix Chaos Gorilla's 'rebalance to healthy zones with no user-visible impact' precedent.
task_spec.output: wrr_select_with_one_unhealthy(A:5,B:3(unhealthy),C:2, n=10000)=ratio(A:C)=2.5000, B selected 0 times; wrr_select_with_one_unhealthy(A:3,B:2(unhealthy),C:1, n=6000)=ratio(A:C)=3.0000, B selected 0 times -- both byte-identical to a baseline Router built with only the healthy deployments configured at the same weights
task_spec.rationale: PASS, verified empirically, not guessed. Built a real gateway/internal/router.Router via New([]Deployment{...}, HealthConfig{}), called ReportProbeResult("B", false) 3x (the real default UnhealthyThreshold) to eject B, then called Select 6000-10000 times across two independently-chosen weight distributions (5:3:2 and 3:2:1, one with a shared-gcd and one with coprime weights) and tallied selections. Compared against a second Router built from scratch with ONLY the two healthy deployments configured at their same weights. task_spec.scenario: The identical Latency-Monkey-style fixed-delay-as-outage injection, but for a STREAMING chat completion request. Assert the same timeout/fallback path activates once the delay is long enough to simulate an outage.
task_spec.output: streaming_upstream_call_timeout=bounded via a real, reset-on-progress idle window, NOT a single whole-call deadline -- dataplane.NewHTTPUpstreamStreamCaller (gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go) now takes an idleTimeout time.Duration parameter; gateway/cmd/gateway/main.go wires it as NewHTTPUpstreamStreamCaller(&http.Client{}, streamIdleTimeout) with streamIdleTimeout=60*time.Second (the non-streaming caller's own 60s magnitude, reused deliberately for consistency, not blindly copied onto the whole call). Internally it derives a cancelable context per call and arms time.AfterFunc(idleTimeout, cancel); the returned body is wrapped in an idleTimeoutReader that calls timer.Reset(idleTimeout) on every real Read. A stall BEFORE headers arrive (client.Do blocked) and a stall MID-STREAM (body Read blocked) are both bounded by the same mechanism -- a legitimately slow-but-still-progressing stream never trips it, since every chunk received resets the window. A pre-headers stall now produces a plain (non-*UpstreamHTTPError) 'context canceled' error that classifyFallbackError classifies as FallbackClassGeneric and attemptFallbackChain walks -- the identical path the non-streaming caller's own 60s timeout already triggers (see the sibling chaos-nonstreaming-timeout-triggers-fallback-on-delay case). A mid-stream stall is bounded the same way but, per streamDeploymentWithFallback's own pre-existing, unrelated design rule (no fallback hop is attempted once any chunk has already reached the client, to avoid duplicating partially-streamed content), does not walk the fallback chain -- it terminates the client-facing stream promptly instead of hanging forever, which is the correct, narrower guarantee for an already-in-flight stream, not a residual gap.
task_spec.rationale: FIXED. Root cause matched this case's own revision-1 finding exactly: gateway/cmd/gateway/main.go wired dataplane.NewHTTPUpstreamStreamCaller(&http.Client{}) with a zero-value Timeout, and streaming.go had zero context.WithTimeout/WithDeadline/SetReadDeadline calls anywhere. Considered and rejected a naive fix first: copying the non-streaming path's single http.Client{Timeout: 60s} onto the whole streaming call would bound total call duration, which is the WRONG shape for a legitimately long-lived SSE connection -- it would kill a slow-but-healthy multi-minute stream exactly as readily as a genuinely stalled one. Implemented instead as a per-call idle window (context.WithCancel + time.AfterFunc, reset via a wrapping idleTimeoutReader on every Read) inside NewHTTPUpstreamStreamCaller, deliberately reusing classifyFallbackError's existing generic-error bucket rather than inventing a streaming-only classification path. task_spec.scenario: Many requests concurrently route through the same deployment while it is genuinely degrading in real time, during the interval between scheduled synthetic health probes -- the AWS DynamoDB/Slack pattern of many independent actors converging on one degrading resource (Findings 3+4), tested against the per-request circuit breaker's own stated scope rather than assumed to cover the cross-request case too. Assert real-traffic failures feed back into router-level health state so concurrent requests stop independently re-attempting a deployment that is failing in real time, without waiting for the next scheduled probe cycle.
task_spec.output: router.ReportProbeResult has exactly one call site in the entire gateway codebase: dataplane.probeOneDeployment, invoked only from the periodic synthetic health-probe loop (RunHealthProbeLoop / ProbeDeployments). No call to attemptFallbackChain, callDeployment, or any real-request failure path anywhere calls ReportProbeResult. Each concurrent request's own attemptFallbackChain circuit breaker (consecutiveFailures) is a fresh, request-local counter declared inside the function body -- zero shared state across concurrent requests. Consequently N concurrently-arriving requests, each independently walking the same fallback chain against a deployment that is failing in real time RIGHT NOW, will each independently retry it up to maxConsecutiveChainFailures (3) times before their own local breaker gives up -- and router.IsHealthy will not reflect that real-time degradation at all until the next scheduled probe cycle accumulates its own UnhealthyThreshold consecutive SYNTHETIC probe failures, a signal entirely decoupled from real traffic outcomes
task_spec.rationale: REAL GAP, honestly named -- a deliberate, already-partially-self-documented scope limit (gateway/internal/router/router.go's own package doc comment: '...the traffic-derived statistical circuit breaker (Envoy-style outlier detection, LiteLLM-style allowed_fails cooldown) -- that class genuinely needs a traffic-volume floor Kelvran doesn't have production data for yet, and correctly stays deferred'), re-verified here directly against the concrete AWS/Slack chaos scenarios rather than assumed still accurate. Confirmed via grep -rn 'ReportProbeResult' across the whole gateway/ tree that dataplane.probeOneDeployment is the ONLY call site outside router's own package. Not fixed in this pass, per this task's scope -- an honest FAIL against the ideal this scenario tests for, distinct from being a newly-discovered surprise bug: the code's own comments already name the general class of gap; this case pins it to the specific, concrete concurrent-convergence shape the research's Findings 3/4 describe.

reference: concurrent requests' real upstream failures feed a shared, real-time health/circuit-breaker signal so that once enough concurrent failures against one deployment are observed, further concurrently-arriving requests stop independently re-attempting it without waiting for the next scheduled synthetic probe cycle to catch up

task_spec.scenario: Cloudflare's own quantified production rate limiter lets traffic run up to roughly 15% over its configured threshold before a separately-cached mitigation flag catches up, because counter increments are processed asynchronously relative to the request path -- a structural TOCTOU gap from decoupling the check from the durable increment (Finding 8). Assert Kelvran's rate limiter, in BOTH in-memory and Redis-backed (distributed) mode, has no equivalent gap.
task_spec.output: in-memory mode: TokenBucket.Allow refills, checks, and decrements while holding one sync.Mutex for the entire sequence (gateway/internal/ratelimit/ratelimit.go) -- confirmed 0% overrun (exactly 1-of-100 admitted) under real concurrent load in the sibling chaos-tokenbucket-race-exact-admission case. Redis mode: gateway/internal/ratelimit/redislimiter's Allow runs exactly ONE atomic Lua script (EVAL/EVALSHA) per call, doing the identical refill-then-decrement math server-side in a single round trip and a single HSET -- Redis's own EVAL execution model runs a script to completion with no other command interleaved on that Redis instance, so there is no window between the check and the increment becoming durable and visible to a concurrent caller, unlike Cloudflare's own explicitly-described 'increment jobs run asynchronously without slowing down the requests' design. Neither Kelvran mode tolerates any measured overrun in the in-memory case (0%, verified); the Redis case's atomicity is a well-documented property of Redis's own single-threaded EVAL execution model, not independently load-tested against a live Redis instance in this pass (this sandbox has no Docker daemon available, confirmed by rootless Docker not found panic from gateway/internal/ratelimit/redislimiter's own real integration TestMain when re-run here)

task_spec.scenario: A rate-limit race lands at the exact moment the caller's primary deployment also fails health checks and its request falls into a fallback_chains walk (Finding 7 combined with Finding 3's cascading-failure shape). Assert the two mechanisms (rate-limiter admission, fallback-chain routing) don't interact to produce a compounded bypass -- e.g. a rejected-then-retried request silently re-entering the bucket via a different fallback hop's own, separately-tracked limit.
task_spec.output: checkRateLimit and checkConcurrency (gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go and streaming.go) are each called exactly once per request, before any deployment is ever selected or any fallback chain is ever walked. attemptFallbackChain (fallback.go) contains zero calls into ratelimit.KeyLimiter.Allow/AllowForModel or ratelimit.ConcurrencyLimiter.Acquire for any of its hops -- its only import from that package is ratelimit.EqualJitterBackoff, used purely for the inter-hop delay's timing math. There is no per-hop, per-deployment rate/concurrency check anywhere in the fallback walk for a request to separately tap into, so no mechanism exists by which walking multiple fallback hops within one request could re-consume the caller's own rate limit or bypass it via a different hop's own, separately-tracked limit -- because no separate hop-level limit exists at all
task_spec.rationale: PASS, verified by direct code reading of the exact call graph. grep -n 'checkRateLimit|checkConcurrency' across dataplane.go/streaming.go shows each is invoked exactly once per HandleChatCompletion/HandleChatCompletionStream call, both strictly before nextDeployment/attemptFallbackChain ever run. grep of fallback.go for ratelimit\. shows the only match is the EqualJitterBackoff call inside the inter-hop-delay branch -- no Allow/AllowForModel/Acquire call anywhere in the file. Since a single logical request (regardless of how many internal fallback hops it tries) consumes exactly one rate-limit token and one concurrency slot from its OWN virtual key -- checked once, upfront -- there is no separate per-deployment or per-hop budget for an attacker to exploit by forcing multiple hops; the scenario's feared 'compounded bypass via a different hop's own separately-tracked limit' has no such separate limit to bypass into in this codebase's current design.

task_spec.scenario: A deployment accumulates a growing streak of consecutive failed active health probes. Assert Kelvran's own background probe loop reduces its probing frequency against that deployment (a backoff/cooldown) rather than continuing to probe it at the exact same fixed interval forever, mirroring the AWS DynamoDB 2015 pattern where continued fixed-rate retries against an already-struggling shared dependency kept it overloaded.
task_spec.citation: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-routing-chaos-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 3 / concrete scenario 7 (AWS's 2015 DynamoDB postmortem: continued retries against an already-degraded shared metadata service are what maintained the overload, fixed only by an operator-triggered pause -- functionally a circuit breaker)
task_spec.output: FIXED. RunHealthProbeLoop (gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go) now drives a new, unexported probeDueDeployments each tick instead of calling ProbeDeployments unconditionally -- ProbeDeployments itself is untouched, still an unconditional, elapsed-time-independent full-pass primitive existing tests rely on, but production's own scheduled loop no longer uses it tick-to-tick. probeDueDeployments checks each deployment's own entry in a new Pipeline-owned probeSchedule map (guarded by a dedicated probeMu; entry type healthProbeSchedule{nextProbeAt time.Time; backoff time.Duration}) and skips any deployment whose own nextProbeAt has not yet arrived, per a new injectable Pipeline.now func() time.Time field (real time.Now in production, mirroring internal/budget.Tracker.now's own convention). Every deployment that IS due is still probed exactly as concurrently, and independently healthProbeCallTimeout-bounded, as ProbeDeployments always did. Immediately after each due deployment's own probe completes, a new rescheduleDeployment helper recomputes its schedule from the FRESH post-probe router.IsHealthy verdict: currently healthy resets backoff to 0 and schedules nextProbeAt = now + interval (the plain configured cadence) unconditionally -- so backoff never applies to a currently-healthy deployment, and a deployment that just crossed back to healthy resumes the plain cadence on its very next scheduling decision, never a lingering backoff. Currently unhealthy grows backoff by a new healthProbeBackoffGrowthFactor constant (=2, deterministic doubling, deliberately not jittered) on every consecutive unhealthy reschedule, capped at a new healthProbeBackoffMaxMultiplier constant (=8) times the configured interval -- so the sequence of successive backed-off intervals is 2x, 4x, 8x, 8x, 8x, ..., never regressing below 2x once unhealthy, never exceeding 8x. At the documented 300s default interval (docs/rfcs/2026-09-07-gateway-active-health-probing.md), a permanently-dead deployment settles into being checked roughly every 40 minutes instead of every 5, materially reducing Kelvran's own probe load against an already-struggling dependency -- exactly the AWS-DynamoDB-postmortem-shaped concern this case names -- while still bounding how long a genuine recovery can go unnoticed. router.go/health.go are byte-for-byte untouched: router.IsHealthy (already exported) was sufficient to read a deployment's current verdict without adding any probe-scheduling concept to that package. Full design rationale, including why the cap is a multiplier of the configured interval rather than a fixed absolute duration and why this stays deterministic rather than jittered (unlike ratelimit.EqualJitterBackoff/RetryBackoff, whose jitter exists to desynchronize many independent CLIENT callers -- a problem that doesn't apply to Kelvran's own single per-instance background loop): docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-health-probe-backoff.md.

Root cause matched this case's own revision-1 finding exactly: RunHealthProbeLoop drove ProbeDeployments off a single flat time.NewTicker(interval) with zero per-deployment state consulted, and ReportProbeResult's consecutiveFailures counter fed no backoff/cooldown signal back to the probe loop at all. Considered and rejected gating backoff on 'accumulated failures below the unhealthy threshold' rather than strictly on router.IsHealthy()==false: the plan's own requirement that backoff must never apply to a currently-healthy deployment directly rules that out, since IsHealthy reports true for a deployment still below the N-of-M threshold -- gating strictly on IsHealthy keeps this a clean additive layer on the existing threshold model rather than a second, parallel one. task_spec.scenario: Many concurrent requests independently observe the same deployment transition from unhealthy to healthy within a narrow window and all route back to it simultaneously, at its full configured weight, with zero ramp-up period -- assert there is no thundering-herd protection on reconvergence, mirroring Slack's 2021 outage where an automated recovery action itself became a second cascading-failure point against a shared dependency.
task_spec.citation: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-routing-chaos-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 4 / concrete scenario 12 (Slack's 2021 postmortem: an automated recovery action -- not client retry behavior -- overwhelmed a shared provisioning dependency, turning recovery itself into a second cascading-failure point)
task_spec.output: a just-recovered deployment no longer receives its full configured weight immediately -- gateway/internal/router/health.go's ReportProbeResult now starts a post-recovery weight ramp on the success that flips h.healthy to true (h.ramping=true, h.rampStep=0), and a new admitRampedTurn (composed into selectHealthy alongside the existing IsHealthy check) applies a Bresenham-style thinning gate so only HealthConfig.RecoveryRampInitialPercent (default 20) of the deployment's own offered turns are admitted at first, ramping linearly to 100% over HealthConfig.RecoveryRampSteps (default 4) further consecutive successful probes -- empirically re-confirmed against the real, now-fixed code via a temporary scratch test (deleted before commit, per this corpus's established verify-then-delete convention), reproducing this case's own original scenario exactly: deployment b (weight 5 of 10 total, a configured 50% share), ejected via 3 consecutive failures (real default UnhealthyThreshold) then recovered via 2 consecutive successes (real default HealthyThreshold) -- the very next 2000 Select calls issued immediately after recovery now measure b at 333/2000 (16.65%), far below its configured 50% share, not the pre-fix 1000/2000 (50.00%); after 4 further consecutive successful probes complete the ramp, an identical 2000-call measurement returns to exactly 1000/2000 (50.00%), proving both the initial dampening and the full return to configured weight once the ramp completes
task_spec.rationale: FIXED. Root cause matched this case's own revision-1 finding exactly: deploymentHealth (health.go) tracked only healthy/consecutiveFailures/consecutiveSuccesses -- no timestamp, cooldown, or 'recently recovered' state at all -- so the moment ReportProbeResult's success branch flipped h.healthy to true, selectHealthy's plain r.IsHealthy(name) check treated the deployment as fully eligible at its complete configured Weight with zero dampening. Fixed by adding ramping/rampStep/rampCredit fields to deploymentHealth and a new admitRampedTurn gate, deliberately layered OUTSIDE wrr.go's own smooth-WRR cursor math (modelState's gcd/maxW/sumW/cw fields are completely untouched) rather than reconstructing the schedule with adjusted weights -- selectHealthy just treats a ramp-rejected offer the same way it already treats an unhealthy one: skip and keep searching within the existing sumW-bounded loop. Ramping is driven by subsequent PROBE OUTCOMES rather than wall-clock time -- a deliberate choice, since router is I/O-free by design with no clock dependency anywhere, and probe-driven ramping gets 'a failure during the ramp restarts it at the initial percentage' for free from the same consecutive-counter machinery UnhealthyThreshold/HealthyThreshold already use. Considered and rejected a weight-rescaling design first (temporarily reconstructing modelState with a reduced integer weight for the ramping deployment): rejected because the common default weight of 1 has no fractional resolution to ramp through, and it would have required resetting the shared WRR cursor on every ramp-step change, distorting the schedule's smoothness guarantee for every OTHER deployment in the group too, not just the ramping one. Re-verified directly against the real, running fixed code, not by editing this fixture to match hoped-for behavior: gateway/internal/router/recovery_ramp_test.go's three new tests (TestSelectGrantsReducedShareImmediatelyAfterRecovery, TestSelectRampShareIncreasesToFullWeightOverRecoveryWindow, TestSelectFullyRampedDeploymentMatchesUnmodifiedProportionalWeightMath -- the last one reusing TestSelectProportionalForWeightedDeployments's own exact 200/100/100-over-400-calls numbers as the backward-compatibility target) all pass, plus a temporary scratch test reproducing this case's own original 2:deployment/weight-5-each/2000-call scenario against HealthConfig{} (real defaults), deleted before commit. Sanity-checked by breaking: temporarily neutered admitRampedTurn to unconditionally return true (the old, no-ramp behavior) and reran the new tests -- TestSelectGrantsReducedShareImmediatelyAfterRecovery and TestSelectRampShareIncreasesToFullWeightOverRecoveryWindow both failed for the right reason (counts["a"] = 300, want 100 -- i.e. the deployment got its full configured share immediately, exactly the bug this fix closes), while TestSelectFullyRampedDeploymentMatchesUnmodifiedProportionalWeightMath correctly still passed (a fully-ramped deployment's behavior is unaffected either way) -- then restored the real fix and confirmed zero git diff trace. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `golangci-lint run ./...` (0 issues), `go run github.com/fe3dback/go-arch-lint@v1.18.0 check` (OK), `gofmt -l .` (empty), `go mod tidy` (empty diff), and `go test ./... -race` (every package ok except the two pre-existing, environment-only rootless-Docker failures, confirmed present on an unmodified checkout too) all pass. Also added health_probe.recovery_ramp_steps/recovery_ramp_initial_percent optional YAML config keys (gateway/internal/gateway/controlplane/config.go, gateway/cmd/gateway/main.go), mirroring unhealthy_threshold/healthy_threshold's own resolution convention, with new controlplane parsing tests.

reference: a just-recovered deployment now receives a gradually ramped share of traffic -- RecoveryRampInitialPercent (default 20%) of its configured weight immediately after recovery, ramping linearly to 100% over RecoveryRampSteps (default 4) further consecutive successful probes -- rather than its full configured weight immediately upon crossing HealthyThreshold, closing the Slack-style thundering-herd reconvergence risk this case originally documented; a probe failure during the ramp window resets it back to the initial percentage rather than letting it keep advancing
